explanations.explanation: Close, but the money part is where this one slips. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet in Judah, says the opposite: "I have neither lent nor borrowed, yet everyone curses me." (Jeremiah 15:10) So no loans, no debts, and he still gets the cold shoulder. That's a rough deal, friend.

That's right, baker. Jeremiah says he has "neither lent nor borrowed," and still everyone curses him. (Jeremiah 15:10) Nobody owes him a dime and he doesn't owe anybody. The cursing comes anyway, and I think that's what stings.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "Surely I will intercede with your enemy in your time of trouble, in your time of distress." (Jeremiah 15:11) He names the trouble and the distress right there, out loud. Then He promises to step in.

Not this time, friend. The text says the LORD will step in. He says, "Surely I will intercede with your enemy in your time of trouble, in your time of distress." (Jeremiah 15:11) That promise comes right in the middle of Jeremiah's complaint, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

explanations.answer: In a land you do not know
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says He will enslave them to their enemies "in a land you do not know." (Jeremiah 15:14) Unfamiliar ground, with no map and no landmarks. Even I'd get lost out there, and I once lost a whole kitchen.

explanations.answer: In a land you have seen before
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the text says, friend. The LORD says the land is one "you do not know." (Jeremiah 15:14) A place they've never seen is a very different picture from one they have. Read that line once more and the answer jumps right out.

explanations.answer: In the land your fathers knew
explanations.explanation: Close to the idea, but the text never says that. The LORD says it will be "in a land you do not know." (Jeremiah 15:14) The passage doesn't mention the fathers here at all. It only says the land is unknown to them.
You got it, baker. Jeremiah prays, "Avenge me against my persecutors." (Jeremiah 15:15) He doesn't dress it up or soften it. I think that's part of why this passage feels so honest.

That sounds gentle, but it isn't what Jeremiah asks. His words are, "Avenge me against my persecutors." (Jeremiah 15:15) He says it plainly to the LORD, with no sugar on top. Not every prayer in the Bible comes out polite.

Nice thought, friend, but the text goes another way. Jeremiah says, "Avenge me against my persecutors." (Jeremiah 15:15) He asks the LORD to act against them. Nothing in that line asks for them to be won over.

Almost, but one word changes it. Jeremiah says, "Know that I endure reproach for Your honor." (Jeremiah 15:15) That's the LORD's honor, not his own. Reproach is hard enough to carry, and he says whose name it's carried for.

That's right, baker. Jeremiah says, "Know that I endure reproach for Your honor." (Jeremiah 15:15) He's speaking to the LORD, so "Your honor" means the LORD's. It's not a prayer about his own reputation.
Yes, baker. Jeremiah says, "Your words were found, and I ate them." (Jeremiah 15:16) No fork, no napkin, just words taken in. He treats them like something he needed.
Not quite, friend. The text says, "Your words were found, and I ate them." (Jeremiah 15:16) Nothing in the verse says he hid them. He took them in.

Hold on, friend, nothing goes up in smoke here. Jeremiah says, "Your words were found, and I ate them." (Jeremiah 15:16) The words are taken in, not destroyed. The next line tells you how he felt about them, and it's a good one.

I get why that sounds right, with all the trouble in this chapter, but it's not what he says. He says, "Your words became my joy and my heart's delight." (Jeremiah 15:16) Joy and delight are the opposite of a heavy burden. The words were a gift to him.

That's right, baker. Jeremiah says, "Your words became my joy and my heart's delight." (Jeremiah 15:16) There's no heavy burden in that line. He's grateful for the words even while the rest of his life is hard.

You got it, baker. Jeremiah says, "I never sat with the band of revelers, nor did I celebrate with them." (Jeremiah 15:17) He stayed out of that crowd completely. The party was happening and he wasn't part of it.

Close, but the text doesn't name them here. Jeremiah says, "I never sat with the band of revelers, nor did I celebrate with them." (Jeremiah 15:17) The people he stayed away from are the revelers, the party crowd.
Good guess, but the elders aren't in this verse. Jeremiah says he never sat with "the band of revelers." (Jeremiah 15:17) That's the group he names, and it's the party crowd.
Yes, baker. Jeremiah says, "Because Your hand was on me, I sat alone." (Jeremiah 15:17) He ties it to the LORD's hand on him. Sitting alone sounds quiet, but I think it was a heavy kind of quiet.
Not in this verse, friend. Jeremiah says, "Because Your hand was on me, I sat alone." (Jeremiah 15:17) The word is "alone," not weeping. The text doesn't say he was crying there.
That's a good picture, but the text doesn't use it. Jeremiah says, "Because Your hand was on me, I sat alone." (Jeremiah 15:17) Nothing here says he was shaking. He just sat by himself.

You got it, baker. Jeremiah tells the LORD, "You have indeed become like a mirage to me—water that is not there." (Jeremiah 15:18) Notice he says "like." He's describing how it feels to him, and he says it right to the LORD.

Not quite, friend. The text says, "You have indeed become like a mirage to me—water that is not there." (Jeremiah 15:18) A stranger isn't in that verse. The picture is water that looks real but isn't there.

That one sounds dramatic, but it's not in the verse. Jeremiah says the LORD has become "like a mirage to me—water that is not there." (Jeremiah 15:18) It's a dry, empty picture. Nothing in the text has a lion in it.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, "If you return, I will restore you; you will stand in My presence." (Jeremiah 15:19) Restore and stand in His presence are both right there in one promise. After all that complaining, that's a lot of welcome.

That one's true, friend, so it takes a flip. The LORD says, "If you return, I will restore you; you will stand in My presence." (Jeremiah 15:19) Both parts are in the verse. It's an "if," but it comes with a promise.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "if you speak words that are noble instead of worthless, you will be My spokesman." (Jeremiah 15:19) A spokesman speaks for Someone else. Good words go with that job.
Not this one, friend. The LORD says, "you will be My spokesman." (Jeremiah 15:19) The job is speaking for the LORD, not guarding anything. The captain's helmet stays on the shelf.
That's a good-sounding job, but it's not the one named. The LORD says, "you will be My spokesman." (Jeremiah 15:19) A spokesman speaks the LORD's words. The verse doesn't make him a judge.
You got it, baker. The LORD says, "It is they who must turn to you, but you must not turn to them." (Jeremiah 15:19) The direction matters here. Jeremiah isn't supposed to bend toward the people.

That one's true, friend. The text says, "It is they who must turn to you, but you must not turn to them." (Jeremiah 15:19) The people turn toward Jeremiah, and he doesn't turn toward them. Check the order of those words and it clicks.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, "Then I will make you a wall to this people, a fortified wall of bronze." (Jeremiah 15:20) A wall of bronze is a lot sturdier than anything my cookie sheets could manage. It's the LORD's promise of strength.
Not clay, friend. The LORD says, "a fortified wall of bronze." (Jeremiah 15:20) Clay cracks, and this wall is built to hold. Bronze is the word in the verse.
Good guess, but cedar isn't in this verse. The LORD says, "a fortified wall of bronze." (Jeremiah 15:20) It's a metal wall, not a wooden one. Bronze is what He names.

I see the thinking, but the text says the reverse. The LORD says, "they will fight against you but will not overcome you." (Jeremiah 15:20) They do fight, and they lose. The promise is that they won't win.
That's right, baker. The LORD says, "they will fight against you but will not overcome you." (Jeremiah 15:20) The fighting does happen. The promise is that they won't overcome him.

explanations.answer: The LORD is with him to save him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, "for I am with you to save and deliver you." (Jeremiah 15:20) That's the reason, and the LORD gives it Himself. The wall holds because He is with Jeremiah.

explanations.answer: The people are too afraid of him
explanations.explanation: Not in the text, friend. The LORD says they won't overcome him "for I am with you to save and deliver you." (Jeremiah 15:20) The reason is the LORD's presence, not the people's fear. The verse never says they're afraid of him.

explanations.answer: The king's guards will protect him
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but no guards show up here. The LORD says, "for I am with you to save and deliver you." (Jeremiah 15:20) The protection comes from the LORD being with him. The verse never mentions the king.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless." (Jeremiah 15:21) Deliver and redeem both mean rescue. The chapter ends on a promise.

Close in spirit, friend, but the verse says something else. The LORD says, "I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless." (Jeremiah 15:21) He promises to deliver and redeem. Hiding isn't mentioned.

That's not what the LORD says here. He says, "I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless." (Jeremiah 15:21) The promise is about rescuing Jeremiah. The verse doesn't say what happens to the wicked.
